buildFreshness.note: Whether a deploy has to build first. Getting this wrong in one direction wastes minutes; in the other it publishes yesterday's site.

rules.when: the built site is older than the teacher's newest content
the built site was made by a PREVIEW
rules.why: **The one that is not obvious.** Serve mode bakes a live-reload client pointed at ws://localhost into every page. Publishing that makes visitors' browsers ask about 'access to other apps and services on this device' — so a preview build is never deploy-fresh, however recent it is. Detected by the built index.html containing 'ws://localhost:'.

rules.when: the built site is newer than the content and was not built by a preview
the built index cannot be read

cloudflareAccountID.why: Trimmed first — a pasted space is not an answer.

cloudflareAccountID.expectProblem: That doesn’t look like an Account ID — it’s 32 letters and digits.
That doesn’t look like an Account ID — it’s 32 letters and digits.
cloudflareAccountID.why: 32 characters but not all hexadecimal — length alone is not the test.

That folder doesn’t exist — use Choose… to pick or create one.

configurationRules.note: What a teacher is told about what they typed. Both apps ask the same questions and must give the same answers; the exact sentences are the product's, so they are asserted by equality rather than by 'contains'.

cases.prompt: First time setup... what is your last name? (letters only):
Please enter letters only for your last name (e.g., 'Gordon'):
Choose a different Netlify site name (or 'q' to cancel):

credentialPrompts.everyRequestNote: An account ID is not a secret and is shown as it is typed; a token is, and is not. Getting that backwards either puts a live credential on a screen a class can see, or hides a code the teacher needs to check they pasted correctly.
credentialPrompts.expiryAdviceIsLoadBearing: Both token steps tell the teacher to set an expiry past the end of the school year. Netlify's box starts at 7 DAYS, and an expired token does not announce itself - publishing simply stops working weeks later, which is diagnosed as the app breaking. Cloudflare's TTL is the same trap. The Cloudflare steps also require choosing 'Include' and the teacher's own account under 'Account Resources': a token that names no account cannot publish, and what comes back does not mention accounts at all.
credentialPrompts.matchedOnWordsNotWholeLine: The two launchers word these prompts slightly differently and are free to keep doing so, so the match is on the words that NAME the credential — 'netlify token', 'cloudflare token', 'cloudflare account id' — not on the whole line.
credentialPrompts.note: Which launcher prompt is a request for a publishing credential, and which one it is. Authored rather than read out of the code, because this is the half that must fail when the matching changes: a prompt that stops being recognised does not crash anything — the teacher simply gets the old one-line question back and no way to answer it.
credentialPrompts.theHelpVariantIsNeverMatched: cloudflareAccountIDHelp carries the SAME steps and link as cloudflareAccountID and differs only in why it is asking, so it must never be returned by the prompt matching: it is opened by a teacher pressing a button beside the Account ID field in Course Settings or the new-course wizard, possibly before any token exists, so it must not talk about 'the token you just made'. Both apps should share one list of steps between the two rather than copying it, because the steps are the half that must not drift.
credentialPrompts.whyNoBrowserOpens: The launchers used to run `open` (macOS) or `Start-Process` (Windows) on the token page the moment they asked, so a browser tab appeared unasked while the teacher was looking at the app. Reported as disconcerting: an application that takes over the screen reads as something going wrong, not as help. The address is now offered as a link in the dialog and printed in the launcher's own output, and the teacher decides when to follow it. Neither app may open a page on the teacher's behalf here.

credentialRequests.note: What a teacher reads when a first publish stops to ask for a Netlify or Cloudflare credential. The launcher's own prompt is one line — "Paste Netlify token:" — which names something most teachers have never heard of and does not say where to get one, so both apps answer it with a dialog: what the credential is for, the steps that produce one, and the page to make it on as a LINK. The link is never opened for them; see credentialPrompts.whyNoBrowserOpens.

requests.explanation: Netlify hosts this section's website for free, and it needs to know that the publishing is coming from you. It does that with an access token — a long code that acts like a password made just for this app. Creating one takes about a minute, and you will not be asked again: it is saved securely on this computer.
requests.name: netlifyToken
steps: Open the Netlify page linked below, and sign in if you are asked to.
Choose “New access token”.
Describe it as something you will recognise later, such as “Class websites”.

Change the expiry — it starts at 7 days. A token that expires stops your publishing working, with nothing on screen to say why, so set a date after the end of your school year: next July is a safe choice. Choose “No expiration” instead if it is offered.
Choose “Generate token”, then copy the long code Netlify shows you — it is only shown once.
Paste it below.
requests.title: Connect to Netlify

requests.explanation: Cloudflare hosts this section's website for free, and it needs to know that the publishing is coming from you. It does that with an API token — a long code that acts like a password made just for this app. Creating one takes about two minutes, and you will not be asked again: it is saved securely on this computer.
requests.name: cloudflareToken
steps: Open the Cloudflare page linked below, and sign in if you are asked to.
Choose “Create Token”, then “Create Custom Token”.
Name it something you will recognise later, such as “Class websites”.
Give it one permission, chosen from the three dropdowns: Account, then Cloudflare Pages, then Edit.

Under “Account Resources”, choose “Include” and then your own account by name. A token that names no account cannot publish anything, and what you get back if you skip this does not mention accounts at all.

Under “TTL”, set the end date to after the end of your school year — next July is a safe choice — or leave it with no end date. An expired token stops your publishing working, with nothing on screen to say why.
Choose “Continue to summary”, then “Create Token”.
Copy the long code Cloudflare shows you — it is only shown once — and paste it below.
requests.title: Connect to Cloudflare

requests.explanation: The token you just made is allowed to publish, but not to look up which Cloudflare account it belongs to — so the account's ID is needed as well. This is the only time you will be asked for it.
requests.name: cloudflareAccountID
steps: Open the Cloudflare dashboard linked below, and sign in if you are asked to.
Choose “Workers & Pages” from the list on the left.
Find “Account ID” on the right-hand side, and copy it.
Paste it below. (It is also the long code in your browser's address bar, just after dash.cloudflare.com/.)
requests.title: One more thing from Cloudflare

requests.explanation: Cloudflare gives every account a 32-character ID, and it says which account your class websites are published into. It identifies you rather than a class, so you enter it once here and every course published to Cloudflare uses it.
requests.name: cloudflareAccountIDHelp
steps: Open the Cloudflare dashboard linked below, and sign in if you are asked to.
Choose “Workers & Pages” from the list on the left.
Find “Account ID” on the right-hand side, and copy it.
Paste it below. (It is also the long code in your browser's address bar, just after dash.cloudflare.com/.)
requests.title: Where to find your Account ID

requests.explanation: Your surname is used to create a clear, recognizable web address for your students and families (such as mcv4u-s1-2026-gordon), and to prevent naming conflicts with other classes. It is saved on this computer and only asked once.
requests.name: teacherSurname
steps: Type your surname below using letters only (for example, “Gordon”).
It will be combined with course codes and the school year to name your class websites.
requests.title: Teacher Surname

requests.explanation: Every website published to Netlify (*.netlify.app) or Cloudflare Pages (*.pages.dev) needs a unique web address. On Netlify, this name is shared globally with all users across the world.
requests.name: siteName
steps: Standard address (recommended): <course>-s<section>-<year>-<surname> (e.g. mcv4u-s1-2026-gordon)
With school abbreviation: <school>-<course>-s<section>-<year>-<surname> (e.g. lcs-mcv4u-s1-2026-gordon)
Use only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens.
requests.title: Choose a Website Address

requests.explanation: That website address is already in use by another site on Netlify. You can add a number suffix or include your school's initials to make it unique.
requests.name: siteNameConflict
steps: Add a number suffix (such as -01, pre-filled below).
Or add your school's initials (e.g. lcs-mcv4u-s1-2026-gordon).
Use only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens.
requests.title: Website Address Already Taken

cases.name: Netlify, the default, passes no target flag
Cloudflare passes the target and the account
Cloudflare with no account ID still names the target
cases.why: The launcher can discover the account from some tokens. A token scoped only to Pages cannot, which is why the app hands over what the teacher gave it — but an empty value must not be passed as an argument.

cases.name: A local folder wins over everything else
cases.why: A folder deploy never touches a web host, so no target and no account are passed even when an account ID exists.

deployArguments.note: Given a course's configuration, what deploy.sh is asked to do. One place must decide this in each app — on the mac it is DeployCommand.arguments, shared by the Deploy button, the assistant and the scheduled-deploy alarm. Built separately anywhere and this happens: the assistant path never passed --target cloudflare, and a Cloudflare course deployed to Netlify. Nothing failed; the site simply appeared on the wrong host. Netlify passes NO target flag at all — it is the launcher's default, and every course written before Cloudflare existed relies on that.

cases.expect: Netlify is limiting how often websites can be deployed right now. Try deploying again in about a minute.
cases.output:
Netlify API error 429: rate limited
Window resets at: 12:04 (in ~59s).
cases.why: Under 90 seconds reads as 'about a minute' rather than '1 minutes'.

cases.expect: Netlify is limiting how often websites can be deployed right now. Try deploying again in about 3 minutes.
cases.output:
rate limit reached
Window resets at: 12:20 (in ~150s).
cases.why: 150s rounds UP to 3 minutes — telling a teacher to come back before the window opens sends them into the same failure twice.

cases.expect: Netlify is limiting how often websites can be deployed right now. Try deploying again in a few minutes.
cases.why: No countdown in the output, so no number is invented.

cases.expect: Your Netlify account isn't connected yet. Add your Netlify access token, then deploy again.
Netlify didn't accept your access token — it may have expired or been removed. Create a new one on Netlify, then deploy again.
Your computer couldn't reach the internet. Check your connection, then try again.
cases.output: curl: (6) Could not resolve host: api.netlify.com

cases.expect: Your computer couldn't reach the internet. Check your connection, then try again.
This website hasn't been built yet. Preview it once, then deploy.
Part of this course folder is a link to another folder, and Windows won't let the website builder follow it. Replace the link with the real folder (the details above name which one), then try again.
cases.output: OSError: [WinError 448] The path cannot be traversed because it contains an untrusted mount point: 'C:\Users\person\Documents\My Course\courses\ICS3U\Media'
cases.why: The toolchain creates no Windows links of its own any more, so this error can only come from a link inside the teacher's OWN folder — commonly the Obsidian trick of sharing one Media folder across vaults with a junction, which current Windows refuses to traverse. The teacher can fix it; the raw OSError reads as a crash. Windows-only output — it can never appear on macOS, and the mac recognises it anyway so that the two explainers stay ONE list of troubles rather than growing a platform switch. (The alternative, a `platform` field on every case, was rejected as machinery for a handful of lines.) This is the only Windows-only case left: three one-time-setup cases sat beside it until 2026-08-20, when the native Windows toolchain removed the launcher lines they matched.

cases.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "build_site.py", line 42
KeyError: 'x'
cases.why: Recognised as nothing, so nothing is said and the app shows the output itself.

failureExplanations.note: A failed task's raw output is written for whoever wrote the tools — API codes, hostnames, stack traces. This turns the ones we recognise into a sentence a teacher can act on. Both apps read the SAME output from the same shared scripts, so both must recognise the same things and say the same words. When nothing is recognised, say NOTHING and show the raw output: an honest fallback beats a confident guess.

generated.note: Written by `Plantoir --write-contracts` from the app's own types and overwritten: credentialRequests, milestones. The rest is hand-written expectation and is preserved.

alsoAccepted.note: Preview flags the launchers accept that the apps do not currently pass. Listed so nobody removes one on the assumption it is dead, and so a new app feature knows what is already there.

deployExtras.meaning: Print what the deploy would do and why it thinks so.
deployExtras.why: A support tool, run by hand when a teacher's deploy misbehaves.

launcherFlags.note: What the APP passes the launchers, beyond the deploy arguments already above. Both platforms drive their own launcher — `preview.sh` here, `preview.ps1` there — and those scripts must accept the same flags, because the apps are written against the same behaviour. A flag renamed in one script and not the other fails at the worst moment: the launcher prints 'Unknown option' and exits, and to a teacher that is a preview that just did not start.

preview.meaning: Build the section's site and STOP. Do not serve it, do not take a port.
usedFor: the assistant's rebuild when no window is open
the build a deploy does first when the built site is stale
preview.why: Serving is the section window's job — it holds the port lease and the web view. A second server started behind its back would take a port the window then could not have.

preview.meaning: Serve on this host port. The websocket goes on port + 1000.
preview.why: The app leases the port, not the script — several previews run at once, one per section, and the app is the only thing that knows which are taken.

preview.meaning: Kill this section's container-side processes and exit. Start nothing.
preview.why: Ending the host-side script leaves the build or server running INSIDE the container. Stop mode reclaims them, and it finds them by working directory — so it catches a running BUILD as well as a server, which is why a stop that has not finished will kill a rebuild that has just started.

setup.meaning: Use this image instead of the one the recipe hash names.
setup.why: Testing a locally built image. `verify.sh` uses it; the apps never do.
For a machine with several (desktop-linux, colima, default).

setup.meaning: Everything after a literal `--` is forwarded to `setup_course.py`.
usedFor: pre-populating a new course: the mac passes `-- --install-example`
setup.why: The launcher owns the container and the Python owns the questions, so anything that is a question for the Python is passed through rather than re-parsed.

launcherFlags.setupNote: **Both scripts also forward an argument they do not recognise**, so `--install-example` alone reaches the Python too — the mac passes the `--` separator and Windows does not, and both work. Checked 2026-08-16 rather than assumed, because the two calls looking different is exactly the kind of thing that turns out to be a silent bug. Pass the separator: it is the documented form in both launchers' help, and it keeps working if either ever starts rejecting unknown flags the way `preview.sh` already does.

browserSafe.note: The address handed to the teacher's browser. Safari tries IPv6 (::1) first for 'localhost' and the container only publishes the port on IPv4, which reads to a teacher as 'the server dropped the connection'. The numeric address sidesteps it entirely. Check whether your default browser has the same behaviour before deciding this is mac-only.

linkRules.note: Two URL rewrites that both apps do, for reasons that are not guessable from the code.

markerOrigins.note: Where each milestone's marker text actually comes from, which decides whether the two apps must match it. shared-python: printed by scripts/*.py, identical on both platforms, so the string must match EXACTLY. launcher: printed by setup.sh/preview.sh/deploy.sh, which have .ps1 counterparts written separately — these deliberately differ, and the mac's 'Setting up this Mac' is Windows' 'Setting up this PC'. elsewhere: printed by the Docker build or a tool, and worth checking by hand. Getting this wrong is silent: a progress bar that stops moving looks like a slow build.

courseCreation.label: Getting ready…
courseCreation.marker: Welcome to the Course Setup Script

milestones.note: label is what a teacher reads; marker is the text in the shared scripts' output that means the step has been reached. The marker is the load-bearing half — it is matched against output produced by shared Python, so both apps must match these strings exactly. A drifted marker does not crash anything: the progress bar simply stops moving, and neither app can tell.

macReference.note: The mac's own answers, for comparison only — do not copy these onto Windows.

modelTiers.note: What must be TRUE of the local assistant's model choice on both platforms. The numbers are NOT shared — a threshold measured on one machine says nothing about another's — but the shape is, and so is every word a teacher sees.

requirements.detail: A smaller assistant and a larger one. Not one, not four.
requirements.why: One rung means either the weakest machine cannot run it or the strongest is wasted. Four means four ladders to re-measure whenever a model, quant or context size changes.

requirements.detail: Read the machine's memory (and whatever else your platform can see) and pick.
requirements.rule: The rung is CHOSEN from the hardware, never asked
requirements.why: A teacher cannot answer 'how much memory does this need?' and should not be asked to. The mac reads physical memory and decides.

requirements.detail: The interface says exactly these, and nothing else.
requirements.rule: The teacher never learns the model's name
requirements.why: A download sheet reading 'Plantoir picked Qwen3 4B to suit this Mac's memory' tells a teacher nothing they can act on and quite a lot about plumbing they never asked about. The real model lives in the filename and the download URL, which are never shown. A mac test fails if a model name, parameter count or file format reaches that string.

requirements.detail: Never inside the container that builds the site.
requirements.rule: The model runs on the HOST, with hardware acceleration
requirements.why: Measured on an M4 Pro, same model and same 3,411-token prompt: 175 seconds inside Colima against 2.1 seconds natively on Metal, and 5.5 tokens/second against 158. That is the largest single number in the feature. See WINDOWS-HANDOFF.md for what to use on Windows.

requirements.detail: Re-run the routing suite when the model, quant or context size changes.
requirements.rule: A model that inverts polarity is VETOED, whatever it scores
requirements.why: An inversion publishes a page the teacher asked to hide — the one failure that reports success. Two 3B-class models were rejected on this alone: Qwen2.5 3B inverted 9 trials in 10, Llama-3.2 3B 10 in 10, on the same sentence.

note: What both apps must agree on outside the assistant. See contracts/README.md.

previewPorts.note: Several previews run at once, one per working folder, and they must not collide. These numbers are the toolchain's, not either app's: the container publishes fixed ports and the host side probes a block.
previewPorts.why: Quartz's live-reload websocket needs its own port (--wsPort = port + 1000). Without it, two previews collide on the websocket even when their site ports differ — which looks like one preview randomly failing to refresh rather than like a port clash.
